lesson.title: When More Begets More: Positive Feedback and the Point of No Return
lesson.summary: Positive feedback loops amplify a change rather than reversing it, driving a process rapidly toward completion, which is why the body reserves them for a small number of events that need a fast, decisive, self-terminating end point.
lesson.body:
Negative feedback loops correct deviations by opposing them, which is why they are so good at holding a variable steady. Positive feedback loops do the opposite: the output of the system reinforces and amplifies the original change instead of reversing it. That makes positive feedback inherently destabilizing, since the changed variable, once it starts moving, drives itself further and further from where it started rather than settling back down. Because of this, the body uses positive feedback far more sparingly than negative feedback, and only for events that benefit from being pushed rapidly and decisively to completion, and that have some built in way of being switched off once that completion happens.

Childbirth is a textbook example. Late in pregnancy, the baby's head begins pressing against the cervix, stretching it. Stretch receptors in the cervix send a signal to the hypothalamus, which triggers the posterior pituitary to release the hormone oxytocin into the blood. Oxytocin travels to the uterus and stimulates stronger, more frequent contractions. Those contractions push the baby's head against the cervix even harder, stretching it further, which triggers the release of still more oxytocin. Each cycle through the loop makes the next cycle stronger, which is exactly the opposite of what a negative feedback loop would do. The loop keeps escalating until the baby is delivered and the cervix is no longer being stretched, at which point the original stimulus disappears and the loop stops.

Blood clotting works on the same escalating logic. When a blood vessel is damaged, exposed tissue underneath the vessel wall activates platelets and a chain of clotting factors circulating in the blood. Each activated clotting factor in this cascade activates many more molecules of the next factor in line, so the response amplifies rapidly rather than staying at a fixed intensity. That cascade ends with the conversion of fibrinogen into fibrin, which forms a mesh that traps platelets and blood cells into a stable clot. As with childbirth, the loop is self limiting: once the clot physically seals the injury, the trigger for further platelet and clotting factor activation is removed, and the amplifying cycle stops.

The fact that both examples end with the loop being physically shut off is not a coincidence, it is essentially a requirement. A positive feedback loop with no way to stop would keep amplifying indefinitely, which is roughly what happens when clotting factors activate inappropriately away from an injury and clots form where they should not. That danger is precisely why negative feedback, not positive feedback, is the body's default strategy for regulating most physiological variables, and why positive feedback shows up only in these special, self-terminating situations.
